analysis.one_liner: Cuts Pentagon budgets each year until the department passes a clean financial audit.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan bill never got a vote: it sat in the House Armed Services Committee from June 2021 until the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have penalized the Defense Department for failing its financial audits. Every Pentagon office or component that could not show it passed an independent audit with a clean opinion would have lost 0.5% of its budget the first year and 1% each year after, with the money returned to the Treasury for deficit reduction. Pay accounts, reserve and National Guard accounts, and military health care would be exempt, and the President could waive the cut for national security reasons. The Pentagon has never passed a clean audit since the department began full independent audits in 2018, which is the problem this bill was designed to fix.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers generally. The Pentagon's annual budget is over $700 billion, and it has been unable to pass a clean independent audit in any year since full audits began in 2018. The bill creates a financial consequence for that failure: budget cuts at the components that cannot account for their money, with the savings used to reduce the federal deficit. Ordinary taxpayers who fund the department with no visibility into where roughly $800 million to $1.6 billion a year in unaudited spending goes would gain a real enforcement tool.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Comptroller of the Defense Department to certify each year whether a component achieved an unqualified (clean) audit opinion on its full financial statements, and automatically cuts that component's budget by 0.5% the first year and 1.0% each following year it fails [S2][S3].
Sends the cut money to the Treasury General Fund to be used for deficit reduction, so the savings go back to taxpayers rather than being shifted to other defense programs [S2][S3].

Protects troops from the cuts: military personnel, reserve, National Guard, and Defense Health Program accounts are excluded, and the President can waive any cut that would harm national security or deployed troops [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The Defense Department components that cannot pass an audit, and the defense contractors whose contracts are funded through those components' budgets. A 0.5% to 1% across-the-board cut applied to every program in a failing component would reduce procurement and operations money, which flows largely to contract spending. Defense-dependent communities and employees would feel any shrinkage in that spending.
analysis.who_pays_short: Unaudited Pentagon programs and defense contractors

drawbacks.text: The cut is blunt: it applies pro rata across every program, project, and activity of a failing component, so it cannot distinguish waste from worthwhile programs, and any actual waste is unknown precisely because the books cannot be audited [S3].
The President can waive the cuts simply by certifying a national-security impact and filing a report, so any administration could nullify the enforcement mechanism if it chose [S2][S3].

The savings are modest relative to the Pentagon budget — well under 1% — and go to deficit reduction rather than to any domestic priority, which limited the bill's upside even for supporters who wanted accountability more than cuts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was a modest, carefully designed accountability tool rather than a budget cutter: the cuts are small, troops and military health care are protected, and a waiver exists for genuine emergencies. Its real value would have been creating a financial reason for the Pentagon to finally fix its bookkeeping. The honest costs are that the cuts are indiscriminate within a failing component, the savings are small, and the presidential waiver could gut the mechanism. On balance it was a low-cost way to pressure the Pentagon toward accountability, but it was never tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with a bipartisan pair of sponsors and referred to the House Armed Services Committee, which never took it up, so it died in committee when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Barbara Lee of California introduced the bill on June 30, 2021, with Representative Michael Burgess of Texas joining as an original cosponsor [S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Armed Services the day it was introduced [S1][S5].
The committee took no further action: no markup, no vote, no report to the floor, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].
It drew 17 cosponsors, 12 Democrats and 5 Republicans, in the House [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pentagon components that fail their audits each year kept their full budgets with no penalty, and the defense contractors funded through those budgets faced no audit-related cuts.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Unaudited Pentagon offices and their contractors

for.what_they_did: Introduced the Audit the Pentagon Act on June 30, 2021.

for.name: Rep. Michael Burgess
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill as an original cosponsor at introduction, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: House Armed Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Rep. Adam Smith (D-WA)
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill: no markup, no vote, no report to the floor in the roughly 18 months before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan — the Republican co-introduced the bill and the 17 cosponsors split 12 Democrats and 5 Republicans — but the bill never reached a vote, so no partisan roll-call exists; the barrier was committee inaction, not party division.

industries.note: Contractor revenue comes largely from Pentagon procurement and operations budgets, so automatic cuts of 0.5% to 1% at any component that fails an audit would trim contract spending, with the savings returned to taxpayers for deficit reduction. The status quo that the bill failed to change — no clean Pentagon audit since full audits began — leaves contract spending in unaudited components untouched.

Any cut to Pentagon program budgets would reduce contract activity in districts and states that depend on defense jobs, which is why across-the-board cuts to failing components carry real local costs. The exclusion of military personnel accounts would have spared service members' pay and health care from these cuts [S3].
